The world is constantly inventing; genius serves all the purposes of human desire. Can faith not invent too, and reach by some new means the outcasts who lie perishing around us? It was the presence of Jesus which inspired victorious courage in the four men carrying the paralytic; is the Lord not among us now? Have we seen His face for ourselves this morning? Have we felt His healing power in our own souls? If so, then through door, through window, or through roof, let us, breaking through all obstacles, work to bring poor souls to Jesus. All means are good and fitting when faith and love are truly set on winning souls. If hunger for bread can break through stone walls, surely hunger for souls is not to be hindered in its efforts. O Lord, make us quick to devise methods of reaching Your poor sin-sick ones, and bold to carry them out at all costs.

e.verse: ...they are agitated like the sea; their anxiety cannot be calmed.
paras: How little we know what sorrow and anxiety may be upon the sea at this moment! We are safe in our quiet room, but far away on the salt sea the hurricane may be cruelly seeking the lives of men. Hear how the winds of death howl through the rigging, and how every timber groans as the waves beat like battering rams upon the vessel! God help you, poor drenched and wearied ones! My prayer goes up to the great Lord of sea and land, that He will calm the storm to a whisper, and guide you to the harbor you desire! Nor ought I to offer prayer alone; I should try to benefit those hardy men who risk their lives so constantly. Have I ever done anything for them? What can I do? How often does the tempestuous sea swallow up the mariner! Thousands of corpses lie where pearls lie deep. There is death-sorrow on the sea, which is echoed in the long wail of widows and orphans. The salt of the sea is in the eyes of many mothers and wives. Remorseless billows, you have devoured the love of women and the support of households! What a resurrection there will be from the caverns of the deep when the sea gives up its dead! Until then there will be sorrow and unrest on the sea. As if in sympathy with the woes of earth, the sea is forever fretting along a thousand shores, wailing with a sorrowful cry like its own birds, booming with a hollow crash of unrest, raving with uproarious discontent, chafing with hoarse wrath, or clattering with the voices of ten thousand murmuring pebbles. The roar of the sea may be joyous to a rejoicing spirit, but to the child of sorrow the wide, wide ocean is even more forlorn than the wide, wide world. This is not our place of rest, and the restless billows tell us so. There is a land where the sea is no more—our faces are steadfastly set toward it; we are going to the place of which the Lord has spoken. Until then, we cast our sorrows on the Lord Who trod the sea of old, and Who makes a way for His people through its depths.

m.verse: ...your fruit comes from Me.
paras: Our fruit comes from our God as to union. The fruit of the branch is directly traceable to the root. Sever the connection, and the branch dies, and no fruit is produced. By virtue of our union with Christ we bring forth fruit. Every bunch of grapes has first been in the root; it has passed through the stem, and flowed through the sap vessels, and fashioned itself externally into fruit, but it was first in the stem; so also every good work was first in Christ, and then is brought forth in us. O Christian, prize this precious union with Christ, for it must be the source of all the fruitfulness which you can hope to know. If you were not joined to Jesus Christ, you would be a barren branch indeed.

Our fruit comes from God as to spiritual providence. When the dewdrops fall from heaven, when the cloud looks down from on high and is about to distill its liquid treasure, when the bright sun swells the berries of the cluster, each heavenly gift may whisper to the tree and say, "Your fruit comes from me." The fruit owes much to the root—that is essential to fruitfulness—but it owes very much also to external influences. How much we owe to God's providence of grace, in which He constantly provides us with new life, teaching, consolation, strength, or whatever else we need! To this we owe all our usefulness or virtue.

Our fruit comes from God as to wise cultivation. The gardener's sharp-edged knife promotes the fruitfulness of the tree by thinning the clusters and by cutting off excess shoots. So it is, Christian, with that pruning which the Lord gives to you. "My Father is the keeper of the vineyard. He cuts off every branch in Me that bears no fruit, and every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes to make it even more fruitful." Since our God is the Author of our spiritual graces, let us give to Him all the glory of our salvation.

e.verse: ...and the surpassing greatness of His power to us who believe. These are in accordance with the working of His mighty strength, which He exerted in Christ when He raised Him from the dead...
paras: In the resurrection of Christ, as in our salvation, there was put forth nothing short of a divine power. What shall we say of those who think that conversion is worked by the free will of man, and is due to his own goodness of disposition? When we see the dead rise from the grave by their own power, then we may expect to see ungodly sinners of their own free will turning to Christ. It is not the word preached, nor the word read in itself; all life-giving power proceeds from the Holy Spirit. This power was irresistible. All the soldiers and the high priests could not keep the body of Christ in the tomb; Death itself could not hold Jesus in its bonds; just as irresistible is the power put forth in the believer when he is raised to newness of life. No sin, no corruption, no demons in hell nor sinners upon earth, can stay the hand of God's grace when it intends to convert a man. If God omnipotently says, "You shall," man cannot say, "I will not." Observe that the power which raised Christ from the dead was glorious. It reflected honor upon God and brought dismay upon the hosts of evil. So there is great glory to God in the conversion of every sinner. It was everlasting power. "Since Christ was raised from the dead, He cannot die again; death no longer has dominion over Him." So we, being raised from the dead, do not go back to our dead works nor to our old corruptions, but we live to God. "Because I live, you also will live." "For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God." "Just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life." Lastly, in the text mark the union of the new life with Jesus. The same power which raised the Head works life in the members. What a blessing it is to be made alive together with Christ!

m.verse: ...I will answer and show you great and unsearchable things you do not know.
paras: There are different translations of these words. One version renders it, "I will show you great and fortified things." Another renders it, "Great and reserved things." Now, there are reserved and special things in Christian experience: not all the developments of spiritual life are equally easy to attain. There are the common frames and feelings of repentance, and faith, and joy, and hope, which are enjoyed by the entire family; but there is an upper realm of rapture, of communion, and of conscious union with Christ, which is far from being the common dwelling place of believers. Not all of us have the high privilege of John, to lean upon Jesus' breast; nor of Paul, to be caught up into the third heaven. There are heights in experiential knowledge of the things of God which the falcon's eye of keen insight and philosophical thought has never seen: God alone can bear us there; yet the chariot in which He takes us up, and the fiery steeds by which that chariot is drawn, are prevailing prayers. Prevailing prayer is victorious over the God of mercy: "In his vigor he wrestled with God. Yes, he struggled with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought His favor; he found Him at Bethel and spoke with Him there." Prevailing prayer takes the Christian to Carmel, and enables him to cover heaven with clouds of blessing, and earth with floods of mercy. Prevailing prayer bears the Christian aloft to Pisgah, and shows him the inheritance reserved; it elevates us to Tabor and transfigures us, until in the likeness of our Lord, just as He is, so also are we in this world. If you would reach to something higher than ordinary groveling experience, look to the Rock that is higher than you, and gaze with the eye of faith through the window of persistent prayer. When you open the window on your side, it will not be bolted on the other.

e.verse: Surrounding the throne were twenty-four other thrones, and on these thrones sat twenty-four elders dressed in white...
paras: These representatives of the saints in heaven are said to be around the throne. In the passage in the Song of Songs, where Solomon sings of the King sitting at His table, some render it "a round table." From this, some expositors, I think, without straining the text, have said, "There is an equality among the saints." That idea is conveyed by the equal nearness of the twenty-four elders. The condition of glorified spirits in heaven is that of nearness to Christ, clear vision of His glory, constant access to His court, and intimate fellowship with His person; nor is there any difference in this respect between one saint and another, for all the people of God—apostles, martyrs, ministers, or private and obscure Christians—shall all be seated near the throne, where they shall forever gaze upon their exalted Lord, and be satisfied with His love. They shall all be near to Christ, all captivated by His love, all eating and drinking at the same table with Him, all equally beloved as His favorites and friends, even if not all equally rewarded as servants.

Let believers on earth imitate the saints in heaven in their nearness to Christ. Let us on earth be as the elders are in heaven, sitting around the throne. May Christ be the Object of our thoughts, the center of our lives. How can we endure to live at such a distance from our Beloved? Lord Jesus, draw us nearer to Yourself. Say to us, "Remain in Me, and I will remain in you"; and permit us to sing, "His left hand is under my head, and His right arm embraces me."

O lift me higher, nearer Thee,
And as I rise more pure and meet,
O let my soul's humility
Make me lie lower at Your feet;
Less trusting self, the more I prove
The blessed comfort of Your love.

m.verse: Then Jesus went up on the mountain and called for those He wanted, and they came to Him.
paras: Here was sovereignty. Impatient spirits may fret and fume because they are not called to the highest places in the ministry; but reader, let it be your joy to rejoice that Jesus calls whom He wills. If He shall leave me to be a doorkeeper in His house, I will cheerfully bless Him for His grace in permitting me to do anything in His service. The call of Christ's servants comes from above. Jesus stands on the mountain, forever above the world in holiness, devotion, love, and power. Those whom He calls must go up the mountain to Him; they must seek to rise to His level by living in constant communion with Him. They may not be able to rise to classical honors or attain scholarly eminence, but they must, like Moses, go up into the mountain of God and have intimate fellowship with the unseen God, or they will never be fitted to proclaim the gospel of peace. Jesus went apart to hold high fellowship with the Father, and we must enter into the same divine companionship if we would bless our fellow men. No wonder that the apostles were clothed with power when they came down fresh from the mountain where Jesus was. This morning we must endeavor to ascend the mount of communion, so that there we may be ordained to the lifework for which we are set apart. Let us not see the face of man today until we have seen Jesus. Time spent with Him is laid out at blessed interest. We too shall cast out demons and work wonders if we go down into the world clothed with that divine energy which Christ alone can give. It is of no use going to the Lord's battle until we are armed with heavenly weapons. We must see Jesus; this is essential. At the mercy seat we will linger until He reveals Himself to us as He does not to the world, and until we can truthfully say, "We were with Him on the holy mountain."

e.verse: ...wolves of the night...
paras: While preparing the present book, this particular expression recurred to me so frequently that, to be rid of its constant persistence, I determined to give a page to it. The wolf of the night, infuriated by a day of hunger, was fiercer and more ravenous than he would have been in the morning. May not the furious creature represent our doubts and fears after a day of distraction of mind, losses in business, and perhaps ungenerous taunts from our fellow men? How our thoughts howl in our ears, "Where is your God?" How voracious and greedy they are, swallowing up all suggestions of comfort, and remaining as hungry as before! Great Shepherd, slay these wolves of the night, and bid Your sheep lie down in green pastures, undisturbed by insatiable unbelief. How like wolves of the night are the fiends of hell, for when the flock of Christ is in a day of clouds and darkness, and their sun seems going down, they hurry to tear and devour! They will scarcely attack the Christian in the daylight of faith, but in the gloom of soul-conflict they fall upon him. O You Who laid down Your life for the sheep, preserve them from the fangs of the wolf!

False teachers who craftily and diligently hunt for the precious life, devouring men by their falsehoods, are as dangerous and detestable as wolves of the night. Darkness is their element, deceit is their character, destruction is their end. We are most in danger from them when they wear sheep's clothing. Blessed is he who is kept from them, for thousands are made the prey of savage wolves that enter the fold of the church.

What a wonder of grace it is when fierce persecutors are converted, for then the wolf lives with the lamb, and men of cruel, ungovernable dispositions become gentle and teachable. O Lord, convert many such people; for them we will pray tonight.

m.verse: ...be separate...
paras: The Christian, while in the world, is not to be of the world. He should be distinguished from it in the great aim of his life. To him, "to live" should be "Christ." Whether he eats or drinks, or whatever he does, he should do all to God's glory. You may store up treasure, but store it up in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal. You may strive to be rich, but let your ambition be to be "rich in faith" and good works. You may have pleasure, but when you are cheerful, sing psalms and make music in your hearts to the Lord. In your spirit, as well as in your aim, you should differ from the world. Waiting humbly before God, always conscious of His presence, delighting in communion with Him, and seeking to know His will, you will prove that you are of heavenly birth. And you should be separate from the world in your actions. If a thing is right, though you lose by it, it must be done; if it is wrong, though you would gain by it, you must scorn the sin for your Master's sake. You must have no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them. Walk worthy of your high calling and dignity. Remember, O Christian, that you are a child of the King of kings. Therefore, keep yourself unstained by the world. Do not soil the fingers which are soon to sweep celestial strings; never let these eyes become the windows of lust which are soon to see the King in His beauty; never let those feet be defiled in muddy places, which are soon to walk the golden streets; never let those hearts be filled with pride and bitterness which are soon to be filled with heaven, and to overflow with ecstatic joy.

e.verse: Lead me, O LORD, in Your righteousness because of my enemies...
paras: Very bitter is the hostility of the world against the people of Christ. Men will forgive a thousand faults in others, but they will magnify the most trivial offense in the followers of Jesus. Instead of vainly regretting this, let us turn it to good account, and since so many are watching for our stumbling, let this be a special motive for walking very carefully before God. If we live carelessly, the eagle-eyed world will soon see it, and with its hundred tongues it will spread the story, exaggerated and embellished by the zeal of slander. They will shout triumphantly, "Aha, just what we wanted! See how these Christians act! They are hypocrites to a man." Thus much damage will be done to the cause of Christ, and much insult offered to His name. The cross of Christ is in itself an offense to the world; let us take care that we add no offense of our own. It is "a stumbling block to Jews": let us make sure that we put no stumbling blocks where there are enough already. It is "foolishness to Gentiles": let us not add our folly to give point to the scorn with which the worldly-wise mock the gospel. How watchful we should be over ourselves! How strict with our consciences! In the presence of adversaries who will misrepresent our best deeds, and question our motives where they cannot fault our actions, how careful we should be! Pilgrims travel as suspected persons through Vanity Fair. Not only are we under surveillance, but there are more spies than we are aware of. The spying is everywhere, at home and abroad. If we fall into the enemies' hands, we may sooner expect generosity from a wolf, or mercy from a fiend, than anything like patience with our weaknesses from men who season their unbelief toward God with scandals against His people. O Lord, lead us always, lest our enemies trip us up!

m.verse: The LORD is a jealous and avenging God...
paras: Your Lord is very jealous of your love, O believer. Did He choose you? He cannot bear that you should choose another. Did He buy you with His own blood? He cannot endure that you should think that you are your own, or that you belong to this world. He loved you with such a love that He would not stay in heaven without you; He would sooner die than let you perish, and He cannot endure that anything should stand between your heart's love and Himself. He is very jealous of your trust. He will not permit you to trust in an arm of flesh. He cannot bear that you should dig out broken cisterns when the overflowing fountain is always free to you. When we lean upon Him, He is glad; but when we transfer our dependence to another, when we rely upon our own wisdom, or the wisdom of a friend—worst of all, when we trust in any works of our own—He is displeased, and will discipline us so that He may bring us back to Himself. He is also very jealous of our company. There should be no one with whom we converse so much as with Jesus. To remain in Him alone—this is true love; but to commune with the world, to find sufficient comfort in our earthly pleasures, to prefer even the company of our fellow Christians to secret fellowship with Him—this is grievous to our jealous Lord. He earnestly desires to have us remain in Him, and enjoy constant fellowship with Himself; and many of the trials which He sends us are for the purpose of weaning our hearts from created things, and fixing them more closely upon Himself. Let this jealousy which would keep us near to Christ also be a comfort to us, for if He loves us so much as to care in this way about our love, we may be sure that He will allow nothing to harm us, and will protect us from all our enemies. Oh, that we may have grace today to keep our hearts in sacred devotion for our Beloved alone, with sacred jealousy shutting our eyes to all the fascinations of the world!

e.verse: ...I will sing of Your loving devotion and justice...
paras: Faith triumphs in trial. When reason is thrown into the inner prison, with her feet fastened in the stocks, faith makes the dungeon walls ring with her joyful notes as she cries, "I will sing of Your loving devotion and justice; to You, O Lord, I will sing praises." Faith pulls the black mask from the face of trouble, and discovers the angel beneath. Faith looks up at the cloud, and sees that:

'Tis big with mercy and shall break
In blessings on her head.

There is a subject for song even in the judgments of God toward us. For, first, the trial is not as heavy as it might have been; next, the trouble is not as severe as we deserved to have borne; and our affliction is not as crushing as the burden which others have to carry. Faith sees that in her worst sorrow there is nothing punitive; there is not a drop of God's wrath in it; it is all sent in love. Faith discerns love gleaming like a jewel on the breast of an angry God. Faith says of her grief, "This is a badge of honor, for the child must feel the rod"; and then she sings of the sweet result of her sorrows, because they work for her spiritual good. Indeed, more than that, says Faith, "Our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison." So Faith rides forth on the black horse, conquering and to conquer, trampling down worldly reason and physical sense, and chanting notes of victory amid the thickest of the battle.

All I meet I find assists me
In my path to heavenly joy:
Where, though trials now attend me,
Trials never more annoy.

Blest there with a weight of glory,
Still the path I'll ne'er forget,
But, exulting, cry, it led me
To my blessed Savior's seat.

m.verse: As they pass through the Valley of Baca, they make it a place of springs; even the autumn rain covers it with pools.
paras: This teaches us that the comfort obtained by one person may often prove helpful to another, just as wells would be used by the company who came after. We read some book full of consolation, which is like Jonathan's rod, dripping with honey. Ah, we think, our brother has been here before us, and dug this well for us as well as for himself! Many a "Night of Weeping," "Midnight Harmonies," an "Eternal Day," "A Crook in the Lot," or a "Comfort for Mourners" has been a well dug by a pilgrim for himself, yet has proved quite as useful to others. Especially do we notice this in the Psalms, such as the one beginning, "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" Travelers have been delighted to see the footprint of a man on a barren shore, and we love to see the waymarks of pilgrims while passing through the valley of tears.

The pilgrims dig the well, but, strangely enough, it fills from the top instead of the bottom. We use the means, but the blessing does not spring from the means. We dig a well, but heaven fills it with rain. A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the Lord. The means are connected with the end, but they do not of themselves produce it. See here how the rain covers it with pools, so that the wells become useful as reservoirs for the water; our work is not lost, and yet it does not replace divine help.

Grace may well be compared to rain for its purity, for its refreshing and life-giving influence, for its coming from above alone, and for the sovereignty with which it is given or withheld. May our readers have showers of blessing, and may the wells they have dug be filled with water! Oh, what are means and ordinances without the smile of heaven? They are like clouds without rain, and pools without water. O God of love, open the windows of heaven and pour out for us a blessing!

e.verse: ...This man welcomes sinners...
paras: Observe the condescension of this fact. This Man, Who towers above all other men—holy, innocent, undefiled, and set apart from sinners—this Man welcomes sinners. This Man, Who is none other than the eternal God, before Whom angels veil their faces—this Man welcomes sinners. It requires an angel's tongue to describe such a mighty stoop of love. That any of us should be willing to seek after the lost is nothing wonderful—they are of our own race; but that He, the offended God, against Whom the transgression has been committed, should take upon Himself the form of a servant, and bear the sin of many, and should then be willing to welcome the vilest of the vile—this is marvelous.

"This Man welcomes sinners"; not, however, so that they may remain sinners, but He welcomes them so that He may pardon their sins, justify their persons, cleanse their hearts by His purifying word, preserve their souls by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, and enable them to serve Him, to declare His praise, and to have communion with Him. Into His heart's love He welcomes sinners, lifts them from the ash heap, and wears them as jewels in His crown; snatches them as firebrands from the fire, and preserves them as costly monuments of His mercy. None are so precious in Jesus' sight as the sinners for whom He died. When Jesus welcomes sinners, He does not have some outdoor reception place, no charity shelter where He feeds them as men do passing beggars; rather, He opens the golden gates of His royal heart, and receives the sinner right into Himself—indeed, He admits the humble penitent into personal union and makes him a member of His body, of His flesh, and of His bones. There was never such a welcome as this! This fact is still most certain this evening: He is still welcoming sinners; would to God that sinners would welcome Him!

m.verse: ...And there were other boats with Him.
paras: Jesus was the Lord High Admiral of the sea that night, and His presence preserved the whole fleet. It is good to sail with Jesus, even though it is in a little boat. When we sail in Christ's company, we cannot be certain of fair weather, for great storms may toss the vessel which carries the Lord Himself, and we must not expect to find the sea less tempestuous around our little boat. If we go with Jesus we must be content to fare as He fares; and when the waves are rough for Him, they will be rough for us. It is through tempest and tossing that we shall come to land, as He did before us. When the storm swept over Galilee's dark lake, every face turned pale, and every heart dreaded shipwreck.

When all human help was useless, the sleeping Savior arose, and with a word transformed the fury of the tempest into the deep quiet of a calm; then the little boats were at rest as well as the one which carried the Lord. Jesus is the Star of the Sea; and though there is sorrow upon the sea, when Jesus is on it there is joy too. May our hearts make Jesus their anchor, their rudder, their lighthouse, their lifeboat, and their harbor. His church is the Admiral's flagship; let us follow her movements, and cheer her officers with our presence. He Himself is the great attraction; let us always follow in His wake, watch His signals, steer by His chart, and never fear while He is within call. Not one ship in the fleet will suffer wreck; the great Commander will steer every vessel in safety to the harbor they desire. By faith we will cast off our mooring lines for another day's voyage, and sail forth with Jesus into a sea of tribulation. Winds and waves will not spare us, but they all obey Him; and therefore, whatever squalls may occur outside, faith will feel a blessed calm within. He is always in the center of the weather-beaten company: let us rejoice in Him. His vessel has reached the harbor, and so will ours.

e.verse: Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity. I said, I will confess my transgressions to the LORD, and You forgave the guilt of my sin.
paras: David's grief for sin was bitter. Its effects were visible upon his outward frame: "his bones became brittle"; "his strength was drained as in the summer heat." He could find no remedy until he made a full confession before the throne of heavenly grace. He tells us that for a time he kept silent, and his heart became more and more filled with grief; like a mountain lake whose outlet is blocked up, his soul was swollen with torrents of sorrow. He fashioned excuses; he endeavored to divert his thoughts, but it was all to no purpose; like a festering sore his anguish gathered, and since he would not use the scalpel of confession, his spirit was full of torment, and knew no rest. At last it came to this, that he must return to his God in humble penitence, or die outright; so he hurried to the mercy seat, and there unrolled the scroll of his iniquities before the all-seeing One, acknowledging all the evil of his ways in language such as you read in the fifty-first and other penitential Psalms. Having done this—a work so simple and yet so difficult for pride—he received at once the token of divine forgiveness; the bones which had been crushed were made to rejoice, and he came forth from his private room to sing the blessedness of the man whose transgressions are forgiven. See the value of a grace-worked confession of sin! It is to be prized above all price, for in every case where there is a genuine, gracious confession, mercy is freely given—not because the repentance and confession deserve mercy, but for Christ's sake. Blessed be God, there is always healing for the broken heart; the fountain is always flowing to cleanse us from our sins. Truly, O Lord, You are a "forgiving God, gracious and compassionate"! Therefore we will acknowledge our iniquities.

m.verse: He does not fear bad news...
paras: Christian, you ought not to dread the arrival of bad news; because if you are distressed by it, what do you do more than other men? Other men do not have your God to flee to; they have never proved His faithfulness as you have done, and it is no wonder if they are bowed down with alarm and cowed by fear; yet you profess to be of another spirit; you have been given new birth into a living hope, and your heart lives in heaven and not on earthly things; now, if you are seen to be distracted like other men, what is the value of that grace which you profess to have received? Where is the dignity of that new nature which you claim to possess?

Again, if you should be filled with alarm, as others are, you would doubtless be led into the sins so common to others under trying circumstances. The ungodly, when they are overtaken by bad news, rebel against God; they grumble, and think that God deals harshly with them. Will you fall into that same sin? Will you provoke the Lord as they do?

Moreover, unconverted men often run to wrong means in order to escape from difficulties, and you will be sure to do the same if your mind gives way to the present pressure. Trust in the Lord, and wait patiently for Him. Your wisest course is to do as Moses did at the Red Sea: "Stand firm and see the Lord's salvation." For if you give way to fear when you hear of bad news, you will be unable to meet the trouble with that calm composure which strengthens for duty and sustains under adversity. How can you glorify God if you play the coward? Saints have often sung God's high praises in the fires, but will your doubting and despairing, as if you had no one to help you, magnify the Most High? Then take courage, and relying in sure confidence upon the faithfulness of your covenant God, "do not let your heart be troubled; do not be afraid."

e.verse: ...a people near to Him...
paras: The era of the old covenant was one of distance. When God appeared even to His servant Moses, He said, "Do not come any closer. Take off your sandals"; and when He revealed Himself upon Mount Sinai to His own chosen and separated people, one of the first commands was, "You are to set up a boundary for the people around the mountain." Both in the sacred worship of the tabernacle and of the temple, the thought of distance was always prominent. The mass of the people did not even enter the outer court. Into the inner court none but the priests dared to intrude; while into the innermost place, or the Most Holy Place, the high priest entered only once a year. It was as if the Lord in those early ages would teach man that sin was so utterly loathsome to Him that He must treat men like lepers put outside the camp; and when He came nearest to them, He still made them feel the width of the separation between a holy God and an impure sinner. When the gospel came, we were placed on quite another footing. The word "Go" was exchanged for "Come"; distance gave way to nearness, and we who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Jesus Christ. Incarnate Deity has no wall of fire around it. "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest," is the joyful proclamation of God as He appears in human flesh. No longer does He teach the leper his leprosy by setting him at a distance, but by Himself suffering the penalty of his defilement. What a state of safety and privilege is this nearness to God through Jesus! Do you know it by experience? If you know it, are you living in the power of it? Marvelous is this nearness, yet it is to be followed by a day of greater nearness still, when it will be said, "The dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them." Hasten it, O Lord!

m.verse: ...partakers of the divine nature...
paras: To be a partaker of the divine nature is not, of course, to become God. That cannot be. The essence of Deity cannot be shared by created beings. Between the creature and the Creator there must always be a gulf fixed with respect to essence; yet just as the first man Adam was made in the image of God, so we, by the renewal of the Holy Spirit, are in an even more divine sense made in the image of the Most High, and are partakers of the divine nature. We are, by grace, made like God. "God is love"; we become loving—"Everyone who loves has been born of God." God is truth; we become true, and we love what is true; God is good, and He makes us good by His grace, so that we become the pure in heart who will see God. Moreover, we become partakers of the divine nature in an even higher sense than this—in fact, in as lofty a sense as can be conceived, short of our being absolutely divine. Do we not become members of the body of the divine Person of Christ? Yes, the same blood which flows in the Head flows in the hand; and the same life which gives life to Christ gives life to His people, for "you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God." Indeed, as if this were not enough, we are married to Christ. He has betrothed us to Himself in righteousness and in faithfulness, and he who unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit. Oh, marvelous mystery! We look into it, but who can understand it? One with Jesus—so one with Him that the branch is no more one with the vine than we are a part of the Lord, our Savior, and our Redeemer! While we rejoice in this, let us remember that those who are made partakers of the divine nature will show their high and holy relationship in their dealings with others, and make it evident by their daily conduct and speech that they have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires. Oh, for more divine holiness of life!

e.verse: Am I the sea, or the monster of the deep, that You must keep me under guard?
paras: This was a strange question for Job to ask of the Lord. He felt himself to be too insignificant to be so strictly watched and disciplined, and he hoped that he was not so unruly as to need to be so restrained. The inquiry was natural from one surrounded by such unbearable miseries, but after all, it admits of a very humbling answer. Truly, man is not the sea, but he is even more troublesome and unruly. The sea obediently respects its boundary, and though it is only a belt of sand, it does not cross the limit. Mighty as it is, it hears the divine "this far, but no farther," and when raging most fiercely with tempest it respects the word; yet self-willed man defies heaven and oppresses earth, nor is there any end to this rebellious rage. The sea, obedient to the moon, ebbs and flows with ceaseless regularity, and thus renders an active as well as a passive obedience; yet man, restless beyond his sphere, sleeps within the lines of duty, lazy where he should be active. He will neither come nor go at the divine command, but sullenly prefers to do what he should not, and to leave undone what is required of him. Every drop in the ocean, every beaded bubble, and every frothy foam-flake, every shell and pebble, feels the power of law, and gives way or moves at once. Oh, that our nature were even one-thousandth part as much conformed to the will of God! We call the sea fickle and false, but how constant it is! Since our fathers' days, and the old times before them, the sea is where it was, beating on the same cliffs to the same tune; we know where to find it; it never forsakes its bed, nor changes in its ceaseless roar; yet where is man—vain, fickle man? Can the wise man guess by what folly he will next be lured from his obedience? We need more watching than the rolling sea, and are far more rebellious. Lord, rule us for Your own glory. Amen.

m.verse: ...Bring the boy to Me.
paras: Despairingly, the poor disappointed father turned away from the disciples to their Master. His son was in the worst possible condition, and all means had failed, yet the miserable child was soon delivered from the evil one when the parent in faith obeyed the Lord Jesus' word, "Bring the boy to Me." Children are a precious gift from God, but much anxiety comes with them. They may be a great joy or a great bitterness to their parents; they may be filled with the Spirit of God, or possessed by the spirit of evil. In all cases, the Word of God gives us one prescription for the curing of all their ills: "Bring the boy to Me." Oh, for more agonizing prayer on their behalf while they are still infants! Sin is there; let our prayers begin to attack it. Our cries for our children should precede those cries which mark their actual arrival into a world of sin. In the days of their youth we shall see sad signs of that mute and deaf spirit which will neither pray rightly nor hear the voice of God in the soul, yet Jesus still commands, "Bring them to Me." When they are grown up they may wallow in sin and foam with hostility against God; then, when our hearts are breaking, we should remember the great Physician's words, "Bring them to Me." Never must we cease to pray until they cease to breathe. No case is hopeless while Jesus lives.

The Lord sometimes allows His people to be driven into a corner so that they may know by experience how necessary He is to them. Ungodly children, when they show us our own powerlessness against the depravity of their hearts, drive us to flee to the Strong One for strength, and this is a great blessing to us. Whatever our morning's need may be, let it, like a strong current, carry us to the ocean of divine love. Jesus can soon remove our sorrow; He delights to comfort us. Let us hurry to Him while He waits to meet us.

e.verse: ...Encourage him...
paras: God employs His people to encourage one another. He did not say to an angel, "Gabriel, My servant Joshua is about to lead My people into Canaan—go, encourage him." God never works needless miracles; if His purposes can be accomplished by ordinary means, He will not use miraculous agency. Gabriel would not have been half as well suited for the work as Moses. A brother's sympathy is more precious than an angel's mission. The angel, swift of wing, would have known the Master's command better than the people's temperament. An angel had never experienced the hardness of the road, nor seen the fiery serpents, nor had he led the stiff-necked multitude in the wilderness as Moses had done. We should be glad that God usually works for man through man. It forms a bond of brotherhood, and being mutually dependent on one another, we are united more completely into one family. Brothers, take the text as God's message to you. Work to help others, and especially strive to encourage them. Talk cheerfully to the young and anxious seeker, and lovingly try to remove stumbling blocks out of his way. When you find a spark of grace in the heart, kneel down and blow it into a flame. Leave the young believer to discover the roughness of the road gradually, but tell him of the strength which dwells in God, of the certainty of the promise, and of the joys of communion with Christ. Aim to comfort the sorrowful, and to hearten the despairing. Speak a timely word to sustain the weary, and encourage those who are fearful to go on their way with gladness. God encourages you by His promises; Christ encourages you as He points to the heaven He has won for you, and the Spirit encourages you as He works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose. Imitate divine wisdom, and encourage others, according to the word of this evening.

m.verse: Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit.
paras: The two most important things in our holy religion are the life of faith and the walk of faith. He who rightly understands these is not far from being a master in experiential theology, for they are vital points to a Christian. You will never find true faith unaccompanied by true godliness; on the other hand, you will never discover a truly holy life which does not have for its root a living faith in the righteousness of Christ. Woe to those who seek after the one without the other! There are some who cultivate faith and forget holiness; these may be very high in orthodoxy, but they will be very deep in condemnation, for they suppress the truth by their wickedness; and there are others who have strained after holiness of life, but have denied the faith, like the Pharisees of old, of whom the Master said that they were "like whitewashed tombs." We must have faith, for this is the foundation; we must have holiness of life, for this is the building upon it. Of what use is the mere foundation of a building to a man in the day of tempest? Can he hide himself in it? He needs a house to cover him, as well as a foundation for that house. Even so, we need the building of spiritual life if we would have comfort in the day of doubt. Yet do not seek a holy life without faith, for that would be to erect a house which can afford no permanent shelter, because it has no foundation on a rock. Let faith and life be put together, and, like the two supports of an arch, they will make our godliness enduring. Like light and heat streaming from the same sun, they are equally full of blessing. Like the two pillars of the temple, they are for glory and for beauty. They are two streams from the fountain of grace; two lamps lit with holy fire; two olive trees watered by heavenly care. O Lord, give us today life within, and it will reveal itself outwardly to Your glory.

e.verse: ...and they follow Me.
paras: We should follow our Lord as unhesitatingly as sheep follow their shepherd, for He has a right to lead us wherever He pleases. We are not our own; we were bought at a price—let us recognize the rights of the redeeming blood. The soldier follows his captain, and the servant obeys his master; much more must we follow our Redeemer, to Whom we are a purchased possession. We are not true to our profession of being Christians if we question the command of our Leader and Commander. Submission is our duty; quibbling is our folly. Often our Lord might say to us as He did to Peter, "What is that to you? You follow Me!" Wherever Jesus may lead us, He goes before us. Even if we do not know where we are going, we know with Whom we go. With such a Companion, who will dread the perils of the road? The journey may be long, but His everlasting arms will carry us to the end. The presence of Jesus is the assurance of eternal salvation; because He lives, we also will live. We should follow Christ in simplicity and faith, because the paths in which He leads us all end in glory and immortality. It is true they may not be smooth paths—they may be covered with sharp, flinty trials, yet they lead to "the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God." "All the Lord's ways are loving and faithful to those who keep His covenant." Let us put full trust in our Leader, since we know that, whether in prosperity or adversity, sickness or health, popularity or contempt, His purpose will be worked out, and that purpose will be pure, unmingled good to every heir of mercy. We shall find it sweet to go up the bleak side of the hill with Christ; and when rain and snow blow into our faces, His dear love will make us far more blessed than those who sit at home and warm their hands at the world's fire. To the peak of Amana, to the dens of lions, or to the mountains of leopards, we will follow our Beloved. Precious Jesus, draw us, and we will run after You.

m.verse: It is for freedom that Christ has set us free...
paras: This "freedom" gives us free access to heaven's charter—the Bible. Here is a choice passage, believer: "When you pass through the waters, I will be with you." You are welcome to that. Here is another: "Though the mountains may be removed and the hills may be shaken, My loving devotion will not depart from you"; you are welcome to that. You are a welcome guest at the table of the promises. Scripture is a never-failing treasury filled with boundless stores of grace. It is the bank of heaven; you may draw from it as much as you please, without restraint or hindrance. Come in faith and you are welcome to all covenant blessings. There is not a promise in the Word which will be withheld. In the depths of tribulations let this freedom comfort you; amid waves of distress let it cheer you; when sorrows surround you let it be your comfort. This is your Father's love-token; you are welcome to it at all times. You also have free access to the throne of grace. It is the believer's privilege to have access at all times to his heavenly Father. Whatever our desires, our difficulties, our needs, we are at liberty to spread all before Him. Regardless of how much we may have sinned, we may ask and expect pardon. It means nothing how poor we are; we may plead His promise that He will provide all things needed. We have permission to approach His throne at all times—in midnight's darkest hour, or in noontide's most burning heat. Exercise your right, O believer, and live up to your privilege. You are welcome to all that is treasured up in Christ—wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. Regardless of what your need is, there is fullness of supply in Christ, and it is there for you. Oh, what a "freedom" is yours! Freedom from condemnation, freedom to claim the promises, freedom to approach the throne of grace, and at last freedom to enter heaven!

e.verse: I prayed for this boy...
paras: Devout souls delight to look upon those mercies which they have obtained in answer to supplication, for they can see God's special love in them. When we can name our blessings Samuel, that is, "asked of God," they will be as dear to us as her child was to Hannah. Peninnah had many children, but they came as common blessings unsought in prayer; Hannah's one heaven-given child was far dearer, because he was the fruit of heartfelt pleadings. How sweet was that water to Samson which he found at "the well of him who called"! Bitter wooden cups turn all water bitter, but the cup of prayer puts a sweetness into the drinks it brings. Did we pray for the conversion of our children? How doubly sweet, when they are saved, to see in them our own petitions fulfilled! Better to rejoice over them as the fruit of our pleadings than as the fruit of our bodies. Have we sought from the Lord some choice spiritual gift? When it comes to us it will be wrapped up in the gold cloth of God's faithfulness and truth, and so be doubly precious. Have we petitioned for success in the Lord's work? How joyful is the prosperity which comes flying upon the wings of prayer! It is always best to get blessings into our house in the rightful way, by the door of prayer; then they are blessings indeed, and not temptations. Even when prayer is not answered quickly, the blessings grow all the richer for the delay; the child Jesus was all the more lovely in the eyes of Mary when she found Him after having anxiously searched for Him. What we win by prayer we should dedicate to God, as Hannah dedicated Samuel. The gift came from heaven; let it go to heaven. Prayer brought it, gratitude sang over it; let devotion consecrate it. Here will be a special occasion for saying, "From Your own hand we have given to You." Reader, is prayer your element or your weariness? Which?

m.verse: ...A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!
paras: Gideon ordered his men to do two things: covering up a torch in a clay jar, he commanded them, at an appointed signal, to shatter the jar and let the light shine, and then blow the horn, shouting, "A sword for the Lord and for Gideon! A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!" This is precisely what all Christians must do. First, you must shine; shatter the jar which conceals your light; throw aside the basket which has been hiding your lamp, and shine. Let your light shine before men; let your good deeds be such that when men look upon you, they will know that you have been with Jesus. Then there must be the sound, the blowing of the horn. There must be active efforts for the gathering in of sinners by proclaiming Christ crucified. Take the gospel to them; carry it to their door; put it in their way; do not allow them to escape it; blow the horn right in their ears. Remember that the true battle cry of the church is Gideon's watchword, "A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!" God must do it; it is His own work. Yet we are not to be idle; human means are to be used—"A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!" If we only cry, "A sword for the Lord!" we shall be guilty of an idle presumption; and if we shout, "A sword for Gideon!" alone, we shall show an idolatrous reliance on an arm of flesh; we must blend the two in practical harmony: "A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!" We can do nothing by ourselves, but we can do everything by the help of our God; let us, therefore, in His name determine to go out personally and serve with our flaming torch of holy example, and with our trumpet tones of heartfelt declaration and testimony, and God will be with us, and Midian will be thrown into confusion, and the Lord of Hosts will reign forever and ever.

e.verse: ...and do not rest your hands in the evening...
paras: In the evening of the day opportunities are plentiful: men return from their work, and the zealous soul-winner finds time to tell abroad the love of Jesus. Do I have no evening work for Jesus? If I do not, let me no longer rest my hands from a service which requires abundant work. Sinners are perishing for lack of knowledge; he who loiters may find his garments stained with the blood of souls. Jesus gave both His hands to the nails; how can I keep back one of mine from His blessed work? Night and day He toiled and prayed for me; how can I give a single hour to the pampering of my flesh with luxurious ease? Up, idle heart! Stretch out your hand to work, or lift it up to pray; heaven and hell are in dead earnest, so let me be as well, and this evening sow good seed for the Lord my God.

The evening of life also has its calls. Life is so short that a morning of manhood's vigor and an evening of decline make up the whole of it. To some it seems long, just as a few coins seem like a great sum of money to a poor man. Life is so brief that no man can afford to lose a day. It has been well said that if a great king should bring us a great heap of gold, and tell us to take as much as we could count in a day, we would make a long day of it; we would begin early in the morning, and in the evening we would not rest our hands; yet to win souls is far nobler work—how is it that we so soon withdraw from it? Some are spared to a long evening of flourishing old age; if such is my case, let me use whatever talents I still retain, and to the last hour serve my blessed and faithful Lord. By His grace I will die at my post, and lay down my charge only when I lay down my body. Age may instruct the young, cheer the faint, and encourage the despairing; if evening has less vigorous heat, it should have more calm wisdom; therefore in the evening I will not rest my hands.

m.verse: Yes, I will rejoice in doing them good...
paras: How heart-cheering to the believer is the delight which God has in His saints! We cannot see any reason in ourselves why the Lord should take pleasure in us; we cannot take delight in ourselves, for we often have to groan under our burdens, conscious of our sinfulness and grieving over our unfaithfulness; and we fear that God's people cannot take much delight in us, for they must perceive so many of our imperfections and our follies that they may rather lament our weaknesses than admire our graces. Yet we love to dwell upon this transcendent truth, this glorious mystery: that as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so the Lord rejoices over us. We do not read anywhere that God delights in the cloud-capped mountains or the sparkling stars, but we do read that He rejoices in His whole world, and that He delights in the sons of men. We do not find it written that even angels give His soul delight; nor does He say concerning cherubim and seraphim, "You will be called Hephzibah, for the Lord will take delight in you"; yet He does say all that to poor fallen creatures like ourselves, debased and depraved by sin, but saved, exalted, and glorified by His grace. In what strong language He expresses His delight in His people! Who could have conceived of the eternal One as bursting forth into a song? Yet it is written, "He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing." When He looked upon the world He had made, He saw that "it was very good"; yet when He beheld those who are the purchase of Jesus' blood, His own chosen ones, it seemed as if the great heart of the Infinite could restrain itself no longer, but overflowed in divine exclamations of joy. Should we not utter our grateful response to such a marvelous declaration of His love, and sing, "I will exult in the Lord; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation"?

e.verse: Do not take my soul away with sinners...
paras: Fear made David pray in this way, for something whispered, "Perhaps, after all, you may be taken away with the wicked." That fear, although marred by unbelief, springs mainly from holy anxiety, arising from the remembrance of past sin. Even the pardoned man will ask, "What if at the end my sins should be remembered, and I should be left out of the roll of the saved?" He recalls his present unfruitfulness—so little grace, so little love, so little holiness—and looking forward to the future, he considers his weakness and the many temptations which beset him, and he fears that he may fall and become a prey to the enemy. A sense of sin and present evil, and his prevailing corruptions, compel him to pray, in fear and trembling, "Do not take my soul away with sinners." Reader, if you have prayed this prayer, and if your character is rightly described in the Psalm from which it is taken, you need not be afraid that you will be taken away with sinners. Do you have the two virtues which David had—the outward walk in integrity, and the inward trust in the Lord? Are you resting upon Christ's sacrifice, and can you go about the altar of God with humble hope? If so, rest assured, with the wicked you will never be gathered, for that calamity is impossible. The gathering at the judgment is like with like: "First collect the weeds and tie them in bundles to be burned; then gather the wheat into my barn." If, then, you are like God's people, you shall be with God's people. You cannot be taken away with the wicked, for you are too dearly bought. Redeemed by the blood of Christ, you are His forever, and where He is, there must His people be. You are loved too much to be cast away with the reprobate. Shall one dear to Christ perish? Impossible! Hell cannot hold you! Heaven claims you! Trust in your Surety and do not fear!

m.verse: Let Israel rejoice in their Maker...
paras: Be glad of heart, O believer, but take care that your gladness has its spring in the Lord. You have much cause for gladness in your God, for you can sing with David, "God, my greatest joy." Be glad that the Lord reigns, that the Lord is King! Rejoice that He sits upon the throne, and rules all things! Every attribute of God should become a fresh ray in the sunlight of our gladness. That He is wise should make us glad, knowing as we do our own foolishness. That He is mighty should cause us to rejoice who tremble at our weakness. That He is everlasting should always be a theme of joy when we know that we wither like the grass. That He is unchanging should continually give us a song, since we change every hour. That He is full of grace, that He is overflowing with it, and that this grace in covenant He has given to us; that it is ours to cleanse us, ours to keep us, ours to sanctify us, ours to perfect us, ours to bring us to glory—all this should tend to make us glad in Him. This gladness in God is like a deep river; we have as yet only touched its bank, and we know a little of its clear, sweet, heavenly streams, but farther on the depth is greater, and the current more rushing in its joy. The Christian feels that he may delight himself not only in what God is, but also in all that God has done in the past. The Psalms show us that God's people in ancient times were accustomed to think much of God's actions, and to have a song concerning each of them. So let God's people now recount the deeds of the Lord! Let them tell of His mighty acts, and "sing to the Lord, for He is highly exalted." Nor let them ever cease to sing, for as new mercies flow to them day by day, so should their gladness in the Lord's loving acts in providence and in grace show itself in continual thanksgiving. Be glad, O children of Zion, and rejoice in the Lord your God!

e.verse: ...whenever my heart is faint. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I.
paras: Most of us know what it is to be overwhelmed in heart—emptied as when a man wipes out a bowl and turns it upside down; submerged and capsized on our side like a vessel overcome by the storm. Discoveries of inward corruption will do this, if the Lord permits the great deep of our depravity to become troubled and churn up mire and muck. Disappointments and heartbreaks will do this when wave after wave rolls over us, and we are like a broken shell hurled back and forth by the surf. Blessed be God, at such times we are not without an all-sufficient comfort; our God is the harbor of weather-beaten ships, the refuge of forlorn pilgrims. He is higher than we are—His mercy higher than our sins, His love higher than our thoughts. It is pitiful to see men putting their trust in something lower than themselves; yet our confidence is fixed upon a supremely high and glorious Lord. He is a Rock, since He does not change, and a high Rock, because the tempests which overwhelm us roll far beneath at His feet; He is not disturbed by them, but rules them at His will. If we get under the shelter of this lofty Rock we may defy the hurricane; all is calm on the sheltered side of that towering cliff. Alas, such is the confusion into which the troubled mind is often cast, that we need a pilot to guide us to this divine shelter. Hence the prayer of the text. O Lord, our God, by Your Holy Spirit, teach us the way of faith, and lead us into Your rest. The wind blows us out to sea, and the rudder does not respond to our puny hand; You, You alone can steer us over the sandbar between those sunken rocks, safely into the fair harbor. How dependent we are upon You—we need You to bring us to Yourself. To be wisely directed and steered into safety and peace is Your gift, and Yours alone. Tonight be pleased to deal graciously with Your servants.

m.verse: ...which He has freely given us in the Beloved One.
paras: What a state of privilege! It includes our justification before God, yet the term "acceptance" in the Greek means more than that. It signifies that we are the objects of divine favor—indeed, even of divine delight. How marvelous that we—worms, mortals, sinners—should be the objects of divine love! Yet it is only "in the Beloved One." Some Christians seem to be accepted in their own experience; at least, that is their impression. When their spirit is lively and their hopes are bright, they think God accepts them, for they feel so high, so heavenly-minded, so drawn above the earth! Yet when their souls cleave to the dust, they become the victims of the fear that they are no longer accepted. If they could only see that all their high joys do not exalt them, and all their low discouragements do not really lower them in their Father's sight, but that they stand accepted in One Who never changes, in One Who is always the Beloved of God, always perfect, always without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, how much happier they would be, and how much more they would honor the Savior! Rejoice then, believer, in this: you are accepted "in the Beloved One." You look within, and you say, "There is nothing acceptable here!" Yet look at Christ, and see if there is not everything acceptable there. Your sins trouble you; yet God has cast all your sins behind His back, and you are accepted in the Righteous One. You have to fight with corruption and wrestle with temptation, yet you are already accepted in Him Who has overcome the powers of evil. The devil tempts you; take heart, for he cannot destroy you, since you are accepted in Him Who has crushed Satan's head. Know with full assurance your glorious standing. Even glorified souls are no more accepted than you are. They are only accepted in heaven "in the Beloved One," and you are even now accepted in Christ in the very same way.

e.verse: If You can? echoed Jesus...
paras: A certain man had a demon-possessed son who was afflicted with a mute spirit. The father, having seen the futility of the efforts of the disciples to heal his child, had little or no faith in Christ; therefore, when he was told to bring his son to Him, he said to Jesus, "If You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us." Now there was an "if" in the request, yet the poor trembling father had put the "if" in the wrong place; Jesus Christ, therefore, without commanding him to retract the "if," kindly puts it in its proper position. "No, truly," He seemed to say, "there should be no 'if' about My power, nor concerning My willingness; the 'if' lies somewhere else." "If You can? All things are possible to him who believes!" The man's trust was strengthened; he offered a humble prayer for an increase of faith, and instantly Jesus spoke the word, and the demon was cast out, with a strict command never to return. There is a lesson here which we need to learn. We, like this man, often see that there is an "if" somewhere, yet we are continually blundering by putting it in the wrong place. "If" Jesus can help me—"if" He can give me grace to overcome temptation—"if" He can give me pardon—"if" He can make me successful? No! "If" you can believe, He both can and will. You have misplaced your "if." If you can confidently trust, just as all things are possible to Christ, so all things will be possible to you. Faith rests on God's power, and is robed in God's majesty; it wears the royal apparel and rides on the King's horse, for it is the grace which the King is delighted to honor. Clothing itself with the glorious might of the all-working Spirit, it becomes, in the omnipotence of God, mighty to do, to dare, and to suffer. All things, without limit, are possible to him who believes. My soul, can you believe your Lord tonight?

m.verse: For I was ashamed to ask the king for an escort of soldiers and horsemen to protect us from our enemies on the road, since we had told him, The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him, but His great anger is against all who forsake Him.
paras: An armed escort on many accounts would have been desirable for the pilgrim band, yet a holy sense of shame would not allow Ezra to ask for one. He feared lest the pagan king should think his professions of faith in God were mere hypocrisy, or imagine that the God of Israel was not able to protect His own worshipers. He could not bring his mind to lean on an arm of flesh in a matter so clearly of the Lord, and therefore the caravan set out with no visible protection, guarded by Him Who is the sword and shield of His people. It is to be feared that few believers feel this holy jealousy for God; even those who in a measure walk by faith occasionally mar the luster of their lives by craving help from man. It is a most blessed thing to have no props and no buttresses, but to stand upright on the Rock of Ages, upheld by the Lord alone. Would any believers seek state endowments for their church if they remembered that the Lord is dishonored by their asking for Caesar's aid—as if the Lord could not supply the needs of His own cause? Would we run so hastily to friends and relatives for assistance if we remembered that the Lord is magnified by our implicit reliance upon His arm alone? My soul, rest in God alone. "Yet," says someone, "are means not to be used?" Assuredly they are; yet our fault seldom lies in their neglect; far more frequently it springs out of foolishly trusting in them instead of trusting in God. Few go too far in neglecting human help, yet very many sin greatly in making too much of it. Learn, dear reader, to glorify the Lord by leaving means untried, if by using them you would dishonor the name of the Lord.

e.verse: I sleep, but my heart is awake...
paras: Paradoxes abound in Christian experience, and here is one—the bride was asleep, and yet she was awake. Only he can solve the believer's riddle who has plowed with the heifer of his own experience. The two points in this evening's text are a mournful sleepiness and a hopeful wakefulness. "I sleep." Through the sin that lives in us we may become lax in holy duties, sluggish in religious exercises, dull in spiritual joys, and altogether passive and careless. This is a shameful state for one in whom the life-giving Spirit dwells, and it is dangerous to the highest degree. Even wise virgins sometimes slumber, yet it is high time for all to shake off the bonds of laziness. It is to be feared that many believers lose their strength as Samson lost his locks, while sleeping on the lap of worldly security. With a perishing world around us, to sleep is cruel; with eternity so near at hand, it is madness. Yet none of us are as wide awake as we should be; a few claps of thunder would do us all good, and it may be that, unless we soon rouse ourselves, we shall have them in the form of war, or pestilence, or personal bereavements and losses. Oh, that we may leave forever the couch of physical ease, and go out with burning lamps to meet the coming Bridegroom! "My heart is awake." This is a happy sign. Life is not extinct, though sadly smothered. When our renewed heart struggles against our natural drowsiness, we should be grateful to sovereign grace for keeping a little vitality within this body of death. Jesus will hear our hearts, will help our hearts, will visit our hearts; for the voice of the wakeful heart is really the voice of our Beloved, saying, "Open to Me." Holy zeal will surely unbar the door.

Oh lovely attitude! He stands
With melting heart and laden hands;
My soul forsakes her every sin,
And lets the heavenly Stranger in.

m.verse: ...so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus.
paras: Having been justified through faith, we have peace with God. Conscience accuses no longer. Judgment now decides for the sinner instead of against him. Memory looks back upon past sins with deep sorrow for the sin, and yet with no dread of any penalty to come; for Christ has paid the debt of His people to the last smallest detail, and received the divine receipt; and unless God can be so unjust as to demand double payment for one debt, no soul for whom Jesus died as a Substitute can ever be cast into hell. It seems to be one of the very principles of our enlightened nature to believe that God is just; we feel that it must be so, and this gives us our terror at first; yet is it not marvelous that this very same belief that God is just becomes afterward the pillar of our confidence and peace! If God is just, I, a sinner, alone and without a Substitute, must be punished; yet Jesus stands in my place and is punished for me; and now, if God is just, I, a sinner, standing in Christ, can never be punished. God must change His nature before one soul for whom Jesus was a Substitute can ever by any possibility suffer the lash of the law. Therefore, since Jesus has taken the place of the believer—having rendered a full payment to divine wrath for all that His people ought to have suffered as the result of sin—the believer can shout with glorious triumph, "Who will bring any charge against God's elect?" Not God, for He justifies; not Christ, for He died, "and more than that was raised to life." My hope lives not because I am not a sinner, but because I am a sinner for whom Christ died; my trust is not that I am holy, but that, being unholy, He is my righteousness. My faith rests not upon what I am, or shall be, or feel, or know, but in what Christ is, in what He has done, and in what He is now doing for me. On the lion of justice the fair maiden of hope rides like a queen.

e.verse: ...Who has become for us wisdom from God...
paras: Man's intellect seeks after rest, and by nature seeks it apart from the Lord Jesus Christ. Men of education are prone, even when converted, to look upon the simplicities of the cross of Christ with an eye too little reverent and loving. They are snared in the old net in which the Greeks were caught, and have a craving to mix philosophy with revelation. The temptation with a man of refined thought and high education is to depart from the simple truth of Christ crucified, and to invent, as the phrase goes, a more intellectual doctrine. This led the early Christian churches into Gnosticism, and bewitched them with all sorts of heresies. This is the root of modern rationalism, and the other fine things which in days gone by were so fashionable in Germany, and are now so ensnaring to certain classes of theologians. Whoever you are, good reader, and whatever your education may be, if you belong to the Lord, be assured you will find no rest in philosophical theology. You may accept this dogma of one great thinker, or that dream of another profound reasoner, yet what the chaff is to the wheat, that is what these will be to the pure Word of God. All that reason, when best guided, can find out is only the A B C of truth, and even that lacks certainty, while in Christ Jesus are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. All attempts on the part of Christians to be content with systems such as Unitarian and liberal church thinkers would approve of must fail; true heirs of heaven must come back to the grandly simple reality which makes the plowboy's eye flash with joy, and gladdens the godly poor man's heart—"Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners." Jesus satisfies the most elevated intellect when He is believingly received, yet apart from Him the mind of the regenerate finds no rest. "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge." "All who follow His precepts gain rich understanding."

m.verse: ...the myrtle trees in the hollow...
paras: The vision in this chapter describes the condition of Israel in Zechariah's day; yet when interpreted in its application to us, it describes the church of God as we find it now in the world. The church is compared to a myrtle grove flourishing in a hollow. It is hidden, unobserved, sheltered; courting no honor and attracting no notice from the careless observer. The church, like her Head, has a glory, yet it is concealed from worldly eyes, for the time of her breaking forth in all her splendor has not yet come. The idea of tranquil security is also suggested to us, for the myrtle grove in the valley is still and calm while the storm sweeps over the mountain summits. Tempests spend their force upon the craggy peaks of the Alps, yet down below where the river flows whose streams delight the city of God, the myrtles flourish by the still waters, completely unshaken by the rushing wind. How great is the inward tranquility of God's church! Even when opposed and persecuted, she has a peace which the world does not give, and which, therefore, it cannot take away: the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guards the hearts and minds of God's people. Does the metaphor not powerfully picture the peaceful, continual growth of the saints? The myrtle does not shed her leaves; she is always green; and the church in her worst time still has a blessed freshness of grace about her; indeed, she has sometimes displayed the greatest freshness when her winter has been sharpest. She has prospered most when her adversities have been most severe. Hence the text hints at victory. The myrtle is the emblem of peace, and a significant token of triumph. The brows of conquerors were bound with myrtle and with laurel; and is the church not always victorious? Is not every Christian more than a conqueror through Him Who loved him? Living in peace, do the saints not fall asleep in the arms of victory?

e.verse: Wail, O cypress, for the cedar has fallen...
paras: When in the forest there is heard the crash of a falling oak, it is a sign that the woodsman is at work, and every tree in the whole company may tremble lest tomorrow the sharp edge of the axe should find it out. We are all like trees marked for the axe, and the fall of one should remind us that for every one of us, whether as great as the cedar or as humble as the cypress, the appointed hour is rapidly approaching. I trust we do not, by often hearing of death, become callous to it. May we never be like the birds in the steeple, which build their nests when the bells are tolling, and sleep quietly when the solemn funeral peals are startling the air. May we regard death as the weightiest of all events, and be sobered by its approach. It is shameful for us to amuse ourselves while our eternal destiny hangs by a thread. The sword is out of its scabbard—let us not trifle; it is polished, and the edge is sharp—let us not play with it. He who does not prepare for death is more than an ordinary fool; he is a madman. When the voice of God is heard among the trees of the garden, let fig tree and sycamore, and elm and cedar, alike hear the sound of it.

Be ready, servant of Christ, for your Master comes suddenly, when an ungodly world least expects Him. See to it that you are faithful in His work, for the grave will soon be dug for you. Be ready, parents; see that your children are brought up in the fear of God, for they must soon be orphans; be ready, men of business; take care that your affairs are in order, and that you serve God with all your hearts, for the days of your earthly service will soon be ended, and you will be called to give an account for the things done in the body, whether they are good or whether they are bad. May we all prepare for the judgment seat of the great King with a care which will be rewarded with the gracious commendation, "Well done, good and faithful servant!"

m.verse: Blessed are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD?
paras: He who claims that Christianity makes men miserable is himself an utter stranger to it. It would be strange indeed if it made us wretched, for see to what a position it exalts us! It makes us sons of God. Do you suppose that God will give all the happiness to His enemies, and reserve all the mourning for His own family? Shall His foes have mirth and joy, and shall His own children inherit sorrow and wretchedness? Shall the sinner, who has no part in Christ, call himself rich in happiness, and shall we go mourning as if we were penniless beggars? No, we will rejoice in the Lord always, and glory in our inheritance, for we "did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but we received the Spirit of adoption, by Whom we cry: 'Abba! Father!'" The rod of discipline must rest upon us in our measure, yet it produces for us a peaceful harvest of righteousness; and therefore, by the help of the divine Comforter, we, the "people saved by the Lord," will rejoice in the God of our salvation. We are married to Christ; and will our great Bridegroom permit His bride to linger in constant grief? Our hearts are knit to Him; we are His members, and though for a while we may suffer as our Head once suffered, yet we are even now blessed with every spiritual blessing in Him. We have the pledge of our inheritance in the comforts of the Spirit, which are neither few nor small. Heirs of joy forever, we have foretastes of our portion. There are streaks of the light of joy to herald our eternal sunrise. Our riches are beyond the sea; our city with firm foundations lies on the other side of the river; gleams of glory from the unseen world cheer our hearts and urge us onward. Truly it is said of us, "Blessed are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the Lord?"

e.verse: My beloved put his hand to the latch; my heart pounded for him.
paras: Knocking was not enough, for my heart was too full of sleep, too cold and ungrateful to arise and open the door, yet the touch of His effectual grace has made my soul rouse itself. Oh, the patience of my Beloved, to linger when He found Himself shut out, and me asleep upon the bed of laziness! Oh, the greatness of His patience, to knock and knock again, and to add His voice to His knocking, begging me to open to Him! How could I have refused Him? Base heart, blush and be ashamed! Yet what greatest kindness of all is this, that He becomes His own doorkeeper and unbars the door Himself! Thrice blessed is the hand which stoops to lift the latch and turn the key. Now I see that nothing but my Lord's own power can save such a wretched mass of wickedness as I am; ordinances fail, and even the gospel has no effect upon me until His hand is stretched out. Now, also, I perceive that His hand is effective where all else is unsuccessful; He can open when nothing else will. Blessed be His name, I feel His gracious presence even now. Well may my heart pound for Him when I think of all that He has suffered for me, and of my ungenerous return. I have allowed my affections to wander. I have set up rivals. I have grieved Him. Sweetest and dearest of all beloveds, I have treated You as an unfaithful wife treats her husband. Oh, my cruel sins, my cruel self! What can I do? Tears are a poor display of my repentance; my whole heart boils with indignation at myself. Wretch that I am, to treat my Lord, my All in All, my greatest joy, as though He were a stranger! Jesus, You forgive freely, yet this is not enough; guard me from unfaithfulness in the future. Kiss away these tears, and then cleanse my heart and bind it with sevenfold cords to Yourself, never to wander anymore.

m.verse: The LORD looks down from heaven; He sees all the sons of men.
paras: Perhaps no figure of speech represents God in a more gracious light than when He is spoken of as stooping from His throne and coming down from heaven to attend to the needs and behold the woes of mankind.
